text.p: IAAF president Primo Nebiolo strongly criticised leading athletes who ignored his plea to compete in Monday's symbolic Solidarity meeting when he arrived in the war-ravaged Bosnian capital on Sunday night.

Nebiolo, along with 200 athletes, officials and journalists, had endured an 11-hour journey to fly the 750 kilometres from Milan to Sarajevo where Monday's meeting in the partially rebuilt Kosevo stadium is expected to attract a crowd of 50,000 people.
"There are people strong on the track without courage off the track," Nebiolo said.
"There are young guys here from countries which are not so famous but are countries which have more feeling with other people who have problems like the people of Bosnia.
"We are here to express to the city our love and to explain that we have been following what has been happening -- your tragedy."

Nebiolo had made a personal plea to the sport's top stars to compete in Bosnia on humanitarian grounds, forgoing their usual appearance fees and prize money. But on Sunday only 52 athletes had arrived, although a further 30 indicated they might come on Monday morning.
Among those already in Sarajevo are five current Olympic champions -- but only one from the United States, high jumper Charles Austin.

The other Atlanta gold medallists were Joseph Keter of Kenya, Balasz Kiss of Hungary, Ludmilla Engquist of Sweden and Chioma Ajunwa of Nigeria. Inessa Kravets of Russia is expected to arrive on Monday.

Austin summed up the feeling of the athletes who had arrived when he said: "Sometimes you have to do things in life which are about giving something back and not just about making money. I am very proud to be here."

British high jumper Dalton Grant, visibly moved at the destruction he saw on the drive from the airport to his city-centre hotel, said: "Seeing desolation like that puts what we do in perspective and makes you respect life more."

Enver Ziga, a member of a local organising committee, admitted he was "very disappointed" that more athletes were not taking part in what will be the biggest event staged in Bosnia since the war began in 1992.

"We are very disappointed with the stars who have stayed away but the ones who have come are very brave and they will help us show the world that there is more to Sarajevo than shelling, blood and death. The world will now see something different." Ziga said.
But athletes have been warned to take precautions during their short stay in the city.
A spokesman for the NATO troops said: "Under no circumstances should any athlete out on a training run go on any grass they see, as it is likely to be heavily mined."

The meeting is due to get underway with an opening ceremony at 1440 local time (1240 GMT) and be over by 1715 (1515 GMT) after which the athletes, officials and journalists will leave on three charter flights bound for Rome and Milan.
